title: Your Hard Work Is Invisible - Here’s How to Fix That
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni argues that effort alone does not earn recognition, and that professionals must deliberately make their work visible. She opens with the familiar scene of a late, over-delivered project met with a bare thank-you, then dismantles the old promise that heads-down hard work leads to security. Her anecdotes carry the case: a manager who quietly did her team's work and was exposed only after she left, and Molteni's own choice of a high-visibility executive project over a hidden yearly event, which led to a promotion. The practical move is to understand stakeholders' needs through candid conversation, build networks before they are needed, and let collaboration put other eyes on your work rather than bragging. The piece is a modest, experience-based career essay in the empathy-and-emotional-intelligence vein, and its caution against kindness that costs you is the most useful thread.
points: Effort is not the same as recognition; work nobody sees, however diligent, earns little, so visibility has to be planned as part of professional development.
Quietly absorbing a team's work looks like leadership but is not; the manager who did so left stakeholders believing work was undone once she departed.
Choosing the high-visibility, high-impact project over the hidden one is a strategic decision, illustrated by the author's own promotion.
Collaboration is the humble route to being seen, since people who build reliable networks before they need them end up with others spotlighting their work.
Kindness that harms you invites being taken for granted, so say no to becoming the default slack-picker.
quotes: Work hard, go to school, get married, get a house, have kids, and then retire.

I knew a manager who often stepped in for their team. Once she left, it was discovered to the degree she stepped in - far beyond what anyone thought. Complaints began to roll in from stakeholders to the new manager almost daily since "work was not being done." She was not leading; she was doing her team's work.

First, consider the needs of your stakeholders. This takes a degree of social awareness to assess the environment around you and the needs of those people surrounding you. This requires a willingness to have a candid conversation, curiosity, and empathy. Do not assume; find out.
Doing work in the shadows, the hidden background work to be the "nice person" or "pick up the slack," ultimately does not provide medals. It is okay to pivot and take on the bigger project.
I don't even know who led the once-yearly event. I don't know many people did. People, including me, by no fault of our own, took the leader of the event and their word for granted, as it was hidden.

In Emotional Intelligence by Daniel Goleman, he described a Harvard Business Review study (page 144), that says the the star performers are those who have built reliable networks at work, before they need them.

Remember, it's good to be kind. But if your kindness is harming you, stop. You do not want to be taken for granted. Don't take on more than you can chew in an attempt to be nice. It only hurts you in the end.
